wu: Students play 'Compare Me' in pairs. One student names two items (e.g., 'phone vs. book'), the other says which is 'more useful' and why. Teacher models: 'A phone is more useful than a book because you can call people.'
wuAlt: Students stand in a line; teacher holds up two flashcards (e.g., 'pizza vs. couscous'), students jump left/right to say 'pizza is tastier' or 'couscous is healthier'.
Teacher writes 'Oujda vs. Rabat' on the board; students brainstorm 3 comparisons (e.g., 'Rabat is bigger', 'Oujda is quieter').
pres: Teacher shows 3 city photos (Oujda, Casablanca, Marrakech) and models: 'Casablanca is bigger than Oujda, but Marrakech is far bigger than Casablanca.' Students repeat chorally. Teacher checks: 'Which city is the biggest?'
presAlt: Teacher uses a Venn diagram with 3 circles (sports: football, basketball, tennis); students fill in 'more exciting', 'more popular', 'more fun'.
Teacher tells a short story: 'Last week, I visited three cafes. Cafe A was cheaper than Cafe B, but Cafe C was far cheaper than both.'
prac: Students do 'Comparative Relay' in teams. Each team gets 3 flashcards (e.g., 'Camel vs. Car vs. Bike'). They race to write sentences: 'A car is faster than a bike, but a camel is far slower than a bike.' Teacher monitors for errors.
pracAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid (e.g., 'Find someone who has a bigger phone than you', 'Find someone who thinks math is easier than science').
Teacher gives 3 adjectives (e.g., 'expensive, old, big'); students write 3 sentences comparing their school, a shop, and a park.
ls: Students listen to a 1-minute audio comparing 3 Moroccan cities (Agadir, Fez, Tangier). They tick which is 'busier', 'cheaper', 'more modern'. Teacher plays audio twice; students compare answers in pairs.
re: Students play 'Human Comparatives'. Teacher calls out 3 students (e.g., 'Ali, Sara, Omar'); class shouts: 'Ali is taller than Sara, but Omar is far taller than Ali!'
prod: Students work in groups of 3. Each group chooses 3 Moroccan foods (e.g., tagine, couscous, pastilla). They create a 2-minute presentation comparing them (e.g., 'Tagine is spicier than couscous, but pastilla is far sweeter than both').
rw: Students read a short text comparing 3 football teams (Raja, Wydad, ASFAR). They underline 5 comparatives (e.g., 'Wydad is more famous than ASFAR'). Then, they write 3 sentences comparing 3 local teams.
st: Teacher tells a story: 'Once, three camels raced. The blue camel was faster than the red one, but the yellow camel was far faster than both!' Close with: 'Today we compared three things accurately. Thank you, class!'
g: Teacher calls out comparisons (e.g., 'bigger than a book'); students mark if they have a picture matching.
Students stand in 3 lines; teacher holds up 3 items (e.g., 'pen, ruler, pencil'); each line says a comparison (e.g., 'ruler is longer than pen').
Teams race to write 3 comparatives for 3 words (e.g., 'hot: hotter, hotter than ice, far hotter than snow').
Students get 3 pictures (e.g., 3 rooms); they write 5 comparisons (e.g., 'Room A is tidier than Room B').
Students survey 3 classmates: 'What do you prefer: tea or coffee? Why?' and report back with comparatives.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 5-sentence comparison of 3 Moroccan cities (e.g., 'Agadir is warmer than Oujda, but Marrakech is far warmer than Agadir').
Support learners: use a sentence frame: '_____ is _____ than _____, but _____ is far _____ than _____'.
hw: Write a 10-sentence text comparing 3 Moroccan festivals (Green March, Eid, Independence Day) with 2 paragraphs.
Record a 1-minute video comparing 3 local restaurants (e.g., 'Restaurant A is cheaper than B, but C is far cheaper than A').
Create a poster comparing 3 apps (e.g., TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat) using 5 comparatives.
tip: Use local examples (Moroccan cities, foods, teams) to boost engagement. Teens relate better when comparisons reflect their world.
